title: Recursion and levels
sub: Tree depth in one line and level-by-level traversal with a queue
cards/0/title: A tree in a problem: the words and the signal
cards/0/body:
Maximum Depth of Binary Tree (LeetCode #104). Given the root of a binary tree, return its depth — the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. There are 0 to 10⁴ nodes with values from −100 to 100. An empty tree has depth 0, a single node has depth 1.

The vocabulary interviews use. The root is the node without a parent, a leaf is a node without children. The depth of a node is how many nodes lie on the path from the root to it; the height of the tree h is the largest depth. For a tree of n nodes, h is between ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ (a complete, even tree) and n (a chain: every node has one child). LeetCode encodes a tree as an array level by level, left to right, with null for a missing node.

The signal for recursion: the answer for a node is built from the answers for its subtrees. Depth is 1 plus the larger of the left and right subtree depths. Node sums, node counts, “are two trees the same” and “is the tree balanced” all work the same way.
cards/1/title: A node’s answer comes from its children
cards/1/body:
The solution is one line: an empty tree has depth 0, a non-empty one has 1 + the max of its children’s depths. The recursion goes down to null, and the answers travel bottom-up: a node returns its number only after both children have answered. The order “children first, then the node” is called post-order.

One template covers dozens of problems: (1) what to return for null; (2) ask the left and right subtrees; (3) combine the two answers into the node’s answer. Name steps 1 and 3 and the code writes itself.

An example is Invert Binary Tree (#226): mirror the tree. Step 1: for null, return null. Step 2: invert the left and right subtrees. Step 3: swap the node’s children and return the node. Empty children are swapped too: a null simply moves to the other side. The root swaps its children last, once both subtrees are already mirrored.

Cost. Each node is called once — O(n) time. Memory is the call stack: at any moment it holds the path from the root to the current node, so O(h). On an even tree of 10⁴ nodes that is about 14 frames, on a chain it is 10⁴. The thread stack is small (see the lesson on C# and Unity in the first unit), so in an interview you say: “O(h) memory, O(n) on a degenerate tree”.
cards/2/q: A tree of 10⁴ nodes where every node has only a right child — a chain. How many MaxDepth calls sit on the stack at the deepest moment?
cards/2/options/0: About 10⁴: the stack holds the whole path from the root, and a chain’s path has length n
cards/2/options/1: About 14: recursion depth is log₂ n
cards/2/options/2: Two: the call for a node and the call for its child
cards/2/options/3: About 5000: recursion goes both ways, and half of the calls have already returned
cards/2/explain: Recursion depth equals the height of the tree, and a chain has h = n: 10⁴ frames on the stack plus the call for null at the very bottom. A MaxDepth frame in .NET on x64 is about 50–60 bytes, so 10⁴ frames take about 0.6 MB: it fits into a 1 MB stack, but the margin is thin. Chains of 10⁵–10⁶ nodes need an explicit stack or a level-by-level traversal.
cards/2/wrong/1: log₂ n is the height of an even tree. A chain’s height is n.
cards/2/wrong/2: A call cannot return until its child answers, and the child waits for its own child — frames pile up along the whole path down.
cards/2/wrong/3: There are no left children: calls for null return at once. There is a single path down, and its length is n.
cards/3/task: Step through MaxDepth: root 3, on the left 9 with child 4, on the right 20 with children 15 and 7, and 7 has 8 on its right. Badges show what a node returned, the call stack is below. The rig will stop twice and ask what the code does next.
cards/3/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Enter 20: the root still needs the right answer
cards/3/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Enter 4 again to check its children
cards/3/goal/asks/0/q: 9 returned 2 — the root’s left subtree is done. What does the code do next?
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: The call for 3 has evaluated only the first argument of Math.Max(MaxDepth(left), MaxDepth(right)). Until the right call returns, the root cannot answer: 3 stays on the stack and the recursion goes into 20. Each node is visited once — the code never comes back to 4.
cards/3/goal/asks/1/explain: A node’s depth is one plus the larger of its children’s depths: a root-to-leaf path goes one way only. 1 + 1 + 2 is the number of nodes on a path that turns at 20, a different quantity (you will need it in the maximum path problem). The root then gets 2 from the left and 3 from the right and returns 4.
cards/4/task: The same template in another problem — Invert Binary Tree (#226): null returns null, invert both children first, then swap them. On top is the tree from the previous trace, below is the same tree as the code changes it. The rig will ask twice what the code does next.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Swap the children of 9: 4 moves right, the left becomes null
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Enter 20: the root is waiting for its right subtree
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Leave 9 alone: it has one child, nothing to swap with
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: 4 has returned, and the right child of 9 is null. What does the code do next?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: The call for 9 has asked both children: the left returned 4, the right returned null at once. Both answers are in, so step 3 of the template builds the node’s answer: swap the children, and null is a child like any other. Only then does 9 return and the root go into 20 — children first, then the node, as in MaxDepth.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: Swap its children: 20 to the left, 9 to the right — and return 3
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: Nothing: both subtrees are mirrored, so the whole tree is
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: Go down into 9 again to mirror it in its new place
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: 20 has returned mirrored: 7 on the left, 15 on the right. What does the root 3 do?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: Mirroring the subtrees is not enough: the root still has 9 on the left and 20 on the right. The swap at the root is its own step 3, and only after it is the bottom tree the mirror of the top one. There is no need to go down again: each subtree has been mirrored exactly once, and the swap moves it as a whole. One call per node — O(n) time and O(h) stack, as in MaxDepth.
cards/5/body:
Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (LeetCode #102). Return the node values level by level: a list of lists, each level left to right. For [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7] the answer is [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]. Up to 2000 nodes.

Recursion goes deep: from 9 it dives into 9’s children before it ever reaches 20. That is depth-first search, DFS. To go wide you need a Queue<T> — first in, first out: take a node from the head, put its children at the tail. Nodes then come out exactly level by level — that is breadth-first search, BFS.

How do you separate one level from the next? The trick: at the start of a level, remember queue.Count and take exactly that many nodes. Invariant: before every iteration of the outer loop the queue holds exactly one level, left to right. Children join the tail and wait for their own iteration, and the count taken in advance never reaches them.

Cost. Each node enters and leaves the queue once — O(n). Memory is the widest level w: a complete tree has about half its nodes on the last level, so O(n) in the worst case.
cards/6/explain: An empty tree gives an empty list, not null. The level size is read once, in the for initializer: afterwards Count grows with the children, but k is already counting down exactly this level. Dequeue takes from the head of the queue (Pop belongs to Stack). Children go in left to right — and come out in the same order on the next level.
cards/7/task: Step through the level-order traversal on the same tree. The current level is highlighted, and the queue after it is shown below. The rig will ask what the next level takes.
cards/7/goal/asks/0/q: Level [9, 20] is done, and their children 4, 15, 7 are in the queue. What does the next iteration return, and what stays in the queue?
cards/7/goal/asks/0/explain: size = queue.Count = 3 was read before the loop, so the for takes exactly 4, 15 and 7. When 7 is taken, its child 8 joins the tail, but k has already counted down to zero — 8 becomes level 4. An option with 8 inside is mixed levels: that is what you get when the level size is not fixed in advance.
cards/8/q: On [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7] this code returns [[3, 9], [20, 15], [7]]. Tap the buggy line.
cards/8/explain: The condition k < queue.Count is re-read on every step, while the queue both shrinks (Dequeue) and grows (children). On the first level: 3 is taken, 9 and 20 join, Count = 2, k = 1 < 2 — and 9 lands in the root’s level. Read the level size once before the loop: for (int k = queue.Count; k > 0; k--) or int size = queue.Count.
cards/9/title: DFS or BFS: how to choose
cards/9/body:
Both traversals are O(n) time: every node is visited once. What differs is the order and the memory.

DFS (recursion or an explicit stack) — when a node’s answer is built from its subtrees’ answers: depth, sums, checking a property, a root-to-leaf path. O(h) memory.
BFS (a queue and queue.Count) — when the problem talks about levels or “the nearest”. Average of levels (#637) — the level sum divided by size. Right side view (#199) — the last node of every level, the one taken when k == 1. Zigzag (#103) — reverse every other level. Minimum depth (#111) — BFS stops at the very first leaf, while DFS walks the whole tree.

Memory on the extreme shapes. A chain of n nodes: DFS holds n frames, while the BFS queue always holds one node. A complete tree of 10⁶ nodes: the DFS stack is 20 frames, while the BFS queue reaches about half the nodes by the last level, on the order of 5·10⁵.

The minimum depth trap. A leaf is a node with neither child. The recursion 1 + Math.Min(MinDepth(left), MinDepth(right)) on a node with one child takes 0 from the empty side and returns 1, although that node is not a leaf: on [1, 2] the answer is 2, not 1. An empty side must not enter the minimum. In BFS the leaf check is explicit.
cards/9/deep:
An explicit stack and the three DFS orders. Pre-order (node, left, right) on a Stack<TreeNode>: pop a node, push the right child before the left so the left comes out first. In-order (left, node, right): go left as far as possible pushing nodes, pop the top one, move into its right subtree. Post-order is the hardest: two stacks or a “children done” mark; it is often easier to do pre-order as “node, right, left” and reverse the result.

O(1) memory. Morris traversal does in-order with no stack and no recursion: it temporarily rewires the right pointer of the rightmost node of the left subtree to the current node and restores it on the second pass. O(n) time, O(1) memory, but the tree is modified during the walk — unacceptable in multithreaded code. In an interview it is enough to know it exists.

The queue in .NET. Queue<T> is a ring buffer; when full it doubles and never shrinks on its own. A queue kept in a field and reused between traversals is usually what you want; after a one-off traversal of a huge tree, call TrimExcess().

A tree for Burst. Node classes with references cannot go into Burst or Jobs. The tree is stored as index arrays: NativeArray<int> for left and right children, −1 for no child, values in a parallel array. A complete tree needs no links at all: the children of node i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, as in a heap. The traversal is the same loop with an explicit stack in a NativeList<int>.
cards/10/body:
The scene hierarchy is a tree too, just not a binary one: a Transform has parent, childCount and GetChild(i). “Visit all descendants” in a Unity interview checks two things: recursion depth and garbage.

Hierarchies are usually tens of levels deep, so the stack will not run out. But recursion via foreach (Transform child in t) creates garbage: Transform implements the non-generic IEnumerable, and GetEnumerator returns a new enumerator object — an allocation per node. A loop over GetChild(i) plus a stack or queue kept in a field (with Clear() before each walk) gives a garbage-free traversal. Need the nearest object with a tag by level — use BFS: it finds the shallowest descendant, while DFS finds the first one along a branch. Note that Transform.Find(name) searches only direct children (or a path with “/”), not the whole subtree.

GetComponentsInChildren<T>() walks the object itself and all descendants depth-first, and every call creates a new array; it skips inactive descendants unless you pass includeInactive: true (the object itself is always checked). The list overload, GetComponentsInChildren(list), fills the List<T> you pass, replacing its previous contents: no new array (the list’s internal buffer grows only while its capacity falls short), but the traversal and the engine calls remain. The rule: do not call it in Update; collect once in Awake and rebuild when the hierarchy changes.
cards/10/deep:
Strings from the engine. t.name and t.tag create a new managed string on every read: comparing names in a loop over thousands of objects is garbage every frame. CompareTag compares without allocating. If you must search by name, put the names into a Dictionary<string, Transform> once.

Flat hierarchies. Changing a transform’s position marks all of its descendants as changed, while hierarchies under different roots can be processed by Unity independently, including in parallel. That is why Unity advises against keeping thousands of moving objects under one “folder” parent and against nesting objects without a reason.

Jobs. To work on the positions of many objects in parallel there are TransformAccessArray and IJobParallelForTransform: the job gets access to the transforms without walking the hierarchy on the main thread.
cards/11/q: Each of 200 units calls GetComponentsInChildren<Renderer>() in Update to highlight its model. The profiler shows GC Alloc every frame. What do you do?
cards/11/options/0: Collect the array once in Awake and reuse it; rebuild only when the hierarchy changes
cards/11/options/1: Replace it with your own recursion using foreach over Transform — no array, no garbage
cards/11/options/2: Walk breadth-first instead of depth-first: BFS does not allocate
cards/11/options/3: Nothing: the arrays are small, and the young GC generation is cheap to collect
cards/11/explain: Every call to GetComponentsInChildren<T>() creates a new array: 200 arrays per frame. The set of renderers changes only together with the hierarchy, so collect it once and update it on that event. If rebuilds are frequent, use the list overload — it creates no array.
cards/11/wrong/1: foreach over Transform creates an enumerator at every node — there will be more garbage, not less.
cards/11/wrong/2: The garbage comes from the API, not the traversal order: a new array on every call.
cards/11/wrong/3: Unity’s collector is Boehm, with no generations: every collection walks the whole heap, and garbage every frame brings the next one closer.
cards/12/q: You are solving Level Order Traversal out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: what to return for an empty tree, the order inside a level, how many nodes
cards/12/items/1: Say why plain recursion does not fit: it goes deep, and we need levels — so a queue
cards/12/items/2: Idea: at the start of a level remember queue.Count and take exactly that many nodes
cards/12/items/3: Write the code while stating the invariant: the queue holds exactly one level
cards/12/items/5: Complexity: O(n) time, O(w) memory — up to n/2 on a complete tree
cards/12/items/6: Edge cases: an empty tree, a single node, a chain
cards/12/explain: First the problem, then the choice of traversal and why, then the invariant and the code, a dry run, and only then complexity and edge cases. On a chain the queue holds a single node — a good moment to compare memory with recursion.
cards/13/q: Match the problem with the technique.
cards/13/pairs/1/1: A queue, queue.Count at the start of a level
cards/13/pairs/3/1: The last node of every level
cards/13/pairs/4/1: An explicit stack instead of recursion
